title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
directAnswer: Find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers, in O(n). Dump everything into a hash set, then only start counting a run from a number whose predecessor (x−1) is absent — that number is a sequence start. Walk x, x+1, x+2… while each is in the set. Each number is visited at most twice overall, so it's O(n) despite the nested-looking loops.

remember.formula:
s = set(nums)
best = 0
for x in s:
    if x-1 not in s:        # x is a sequence start
        y = x
        while y+1 in s: y += 1
        best = max(best, y - x + 1)
rules: Only begin a walk when `x-1` is **not** in the set — that's what makes it O(n), not O(n²).
Use a **set** for O(1) membership; iterate the set (not the array) to skip duplicates cheaply.
Walk **upward** (`x+1, x+2…`); each number is the start of at most one walk.
Track the best length as you go; don't sort (sorting is the O(n log n) fallback).
Empty input → answer is 0; handle it before the loop or let `best` stay 0.
whenToUse: Longest run / streak of consecutive values in unordered data
Need O(n) where sorting's O(n log n) is too slow or disallowed
antiSignals: Sequence must preserve original index order → not this (that's subsequence DP)
Need the actual elements / multiple longest runs → adapt to record them
Data already sorted → a single linear scan comparing neighbours suffices
remember.takeaway: The start-check (x−1 absent) is the whole trick: it guarantees each element is touched O(1) amortized times, turning what looks quadratic into linear. It's the same 'remember everything in a set' lever as Two Sum and Contains Duplicate.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can hit O(n) without sorting by using a hash set and the start-of-sequence optimization — and whether you can justify the linear bound despite a while-loop inside a for-loop.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Walking a sequence from every element (O(n²)), or sorting and calling it optimal when O(n) was required.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain the amortized O(n) argument: the inner while loop only runs for sequence starts, and across all starts it visits each element once.

problemStatement:
Given an unsorted array of integers `nums`, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence.

You must write an algorithm that runs in **O(n)** time.
understanding: A 'consecutive sequence' is a set of integers that form an unbroken run like 3,4,5,6 — order in the array is irrelevant, only the values matter. We want the length of the longest such run that can be assembled from the array's values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the sequence have to appear in order in the array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the values matter. [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2] yields the run 1,2,3,4 even though they're scattered.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are duplicates possible, and do they affect the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, duplicates can appear; they don't lengthen a run. Using a set naturally collapses them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What should an empty array return?
Is sorting acceptable?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It gives the right answer in O(n log n), but the problem demands O(n), so we use the hash-set method.

approaches.name: Sort Then Scan
approaches.whenToMention: The intuitive answer — but it's O(n log n), so flag that it misses the O(n) requirement.
hints: If the numbers were in order, how would you measure the longest unbroken run?
Sort, then scan once counting how long each consecutive run lasts, resetting on gaps.
Skip duplicates while scanning. It works, but sorting costs O(n log n) — not the required O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n); the linear scan after is O(n). O(1) extra space if sorting in place.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the array, then sweep left to right. Keep a `current` run length: if the next element is exactly one more than the previous, extend the run; if it's equal, skip it (duplicate); otherwise reset the run to 1. Track the maximum run seen.

**Why mention it.** It's the natural first instinct and is easy to get right. But the problem explicitly asks for O(n), so this is the baseline you improve on with the hash-set method.
approaches.insight: Sorting makes 'consecutive' a local property (adjacent elements), which is easy to scan — but paying O(n log n) to get locality is exactly the cost the hash-set approach avoids.

java.explanation: Skip duplicates so they don't reset or inflate the run.
Exactly one more → the run continues.

python.explanation: A gap broke the run; restart counting from this element.

pitfalls: Not handling duplicates — they can falsely reset or break runs.
Returning 0 for a non-empty array because best wasn't seeded to 1.
Claiming O(n) — sorting makes it O(n log n).

approaches.name: Hash Set — Start-Only Walk (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The required O(n) answer. Lead with the 'only start from sequence beginnings' insight.
hints: Put everything in a set for O(1) membership. How do you avoid recounting the same run from different elements?
A number x begins a sequence only if x-1 is NOT in the set. Start counting just from those.
From each start, walk x+1, x+2… while present. Each element is the start of at most one walk, so total work is O(n).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the set is O(n). The inner while loop only runs for sequence starts, and across all starts it visits each element exactly once, so the loops together are O(n) amortized.
approaches.explanation:
Insert all numbers into a hash set (which also removes duplicates). Then iterate the set; for each value `x`, check whether `x-1` is present. If it is, `x` sits in the middle of some run and we skip it — counting from here would be redundant. If `x-1` is absent, `x` is the smallest element of its run, so we walk upward `x+1, x+2, …` while each is in the set, counting the length, and update the best.

**Why it's O(n), not O(n²).** The nested while loop looks dangerous, but it only ever executes for sequence *starts*. A run of length L has exactly one start, and its while loop runs L steps — visiting each of the run's L elements once. Summed over all runs, that's every element visited a constant number of times: O(n) total.
approaches.insight: The 'x−1 not in set' guard is the linchpin. Without it you'd re-walk the same run from each of its members (quadratic). With it, every element participates in exactly one upward walk. This is the same 'store everything, query in O(1)' trade as Two Sum, applied to neighbour-presence.

steps.note: The longest run found from its true start.

code.python:
def longestConsecutive(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
    num_set = set(nums)
    best = 0
    for x in num_set:
        if x - 1 not in num_set:          # x starts a sequence
            length = 1
            current = x
            while current + 1 in num_set:
                current += 1
                length += 1
            best = max(best, length)
    return best

java.explanation: The O(n) guard — only walk from the smallest element of each run.
Extend upward; each element here belongs to this run only.
Record the longest run discovered so far.

python.line: if x - 1 not in num_set:          # x starts a sequence
python.explanation: Skip mid-run elements so each run is counted once.
Walk the run upward via O(1) membership tests.

diagrams.title: Set membership drives the walk
diagrams.caption: Only x with x-1 absent start a walk; we then probe x+1, x+2…

edgeCases.behavior: Empty set, loop never runs, best stays 0.
Set collapses to {1}; single run of length 1.
Negatives work the same; run -3,-2,-1 has length 3.

pitfalls: Omitting the x-1 guard — degrades to O(n²) by re-walking runs.
Iterating the original array instead of the set — duplicates cause repeated work.
Seeding best to 1 and returning 1 on an empty array — seed to 0.

commonMistakes: Walking a run from every element instead of only from sequence starts (O(n²)).
Sorting and claiming O(n) — it's O(n log n).
Returning 1 for an empty array due to a bad initial value.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the start-of-sequence guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Without checking that x-1 is absent, every element of a run launches its own upward walk, making the algorithm O(n²) and defeating the purpose of the set.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for x in num_set:
    length = 1; cur = x
    while cur + 1 in num_set:   # runs for EVERY x
        cur += 1; length += 1
    best = max(best, length)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Iterating the array, not the set
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping over nums (with duplicates) repeats work and can miscount; iterate the deduplicated set instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.good: for (int x : set) { /* each distinct value once */ }

patternNote: Hash set with a start-of-run guard. Reach for it when you need the longest consecutive run in O(n) on unsorted data. The 'only start from boundaries' trick to keep nested loops linear recurs in grid/island traversals too.
